item.title: Deep diffusion model-based dual structured light for large-format complex surface imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting structured light measures 3D shape with high accuracy by projecting sinusoidal fringes and reading their phase in a camera image. A single projector–camera unit, however, sees an object from only one angle. On large or complex surfaces, protrusions block the projected light or the camera’s view, leaving shadowed and blind regions without phase information, and the measurable area is limited. Measuring from several viewpoints, or turning the object on a turntable, fills the gaps but is slow and impossible for objects that cannot be moved.

Adding a second projector–camera head covers what the first cannot see, but only if the two heads can measure at the same time with overlapping views. When both projectors are on, each camera records the two fringe patterns superimposed in the overlap, an aliased pattern that leads to incorrect reconstruction. Earlier ways of separating such patterns rely on colour filters and special optical paths, extra hardware, orientation or colour multiplexing, or a strict order of projected patterns, and some give up simultaneous measurement altogether.

How it works

The system pairs two synchronised projector–camera heads with locally overlapping fields of view and runs them simultaneously. Instead of preventing the aliasing with hardware, it removes it in software: a conditional diffusion model learns to recover, from each aliased image, the clean fringe pattern of one projector. After that, each head works as a conventional structured-light unit, and the overlap is used to fuse the two results.

  1. Two synchronised heads. Two projectors and two cameras are connected by synchronous control lines, so both heads project and capture at the same time. Each head measures part of the surface, and their fields of view overlap locally.
  2. Aliasing as a sum. In the overlap a camera pixel integrates light from both projectors, so its intensity is the sum of the two projected patterns’ contributions, I(u) = I(u; l1) + I(u; l2) (background light is assumed not to affect the phase). The pattern of one head is therefore I(u; ln) = I(u) − I(u; l3−n), which the authors read as a denoising problem, with the other head’s pattern as the noise.
  3. Conditional diffusion recovers the clean fringe. A U-Net with self-attention is trained in a conditional denoising diffusion framework. Training pairs come from the system itself: one head on alone gives the clean pattern x0, both heads on give the aliased pattern y, which serves as the condition. At inference the model starts from Gaussian noise and denoises it step by step, guided by y, until it reaches the dealiased fringe.
  4. Phase and 3D per head. With clean fringes, the four-step phase-shifting algorithm gives the wrapped phase and multi-frequency heterodyne unwrapping the absolute phase. Triangulation with each head’s calibrated projector and camera parameters then turns it into a partial 3D point cloud.
  5. Fusion with ICP. The overlapping region provides corresponding points, and the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm estimates the rotation and translation that merge the two partial point clouds into the complete surface.

Results

Fringe recovery: PSNR 45.80 dB, MSE 1.85, SSIM 0.98 against the non-aliased fringe pattern (Section 3.2, Fig. 7).
Phase: at most 0.05 rad difference from the phase of the non-aliased pattern along a test row (Fig. 8).
3D: RMS error 0.057 mm for the dealiased reconstruction against a reference from separate, non-aliased measurements (Fig. 9).
Reconstruction error within 8 µm along sampled depth profiles of a prism with prominent protrusions (Fig. 12).

The prototype uses two TJ20U2 projectors and two CMOS cameras with a resolution of 3072 × 2048. Fringe patterns with periods of 100, 110, 120 and 130, each in four phase steps of 0.5π and with varied initial phase, produced 4043 training and 1583 test samples of 512 × 512 pixels; the model was trained with T = 4000 diffusion steps for 800 epochs. Without dealiasing, fringe aliasing introduces significant errors in both heads’ point clouds and in the fused result; with the diffusion model, the object is reconstructed successfully. A derivative-based recovery method from earlier work makes the fringes noticeably denser with local intensity amplification, and its point cloud is noisy with pronounced layering. On a prism chosen to accentuate occlusion, fusion widened the reconstruction range and filled sparse areas that a single head leaves.

The authors define the scope of the evaluation as truly simultaneous dual-head measurement with a local overlap. Other aliasing-removal methods depend on specific hardware or projection schemes, such as colour or orientation multiplexing, optical-path separation or controlled projection sequences, and could not be run on this configuration without changing it. Results are therefore compared with non-aliased single-projector measurements as the reference and with conventional phase shifting applied directly to the aliased fringes as the baseline.

item.title: Self-calibrating structured light three-dimensional imaging method with fringe projection
item.description:
The problem

Industrial inspection asks for 3D measurement that is efficient, economical and highly precise, and structured-light 3D measurement meets these requirements. In a monocular camera–projector system that reconstructs surfaces by phase-shifting fringe projection, long-term operational stability is the key bottleneck for measurement accuracy: external factors such as vibration make the system’s extrinsic parameters move slowly, which weakens the triangulation constraints and lowers the accuracy of the measurement results.

How it works

The paper develops a self-calibrating fringe-projection 3D imaging technique that integrates bundle adjustment. The surface of the object being reconstructed becomes a constraint in the calibration itself.

  1. Drifting extrinsics. Vibration slowly moves the extrinsic parameters of the camera–projector system, weakening the triangulation constraints.
  2. Initial values. The independent calibration parameters of the camera and of the projector serve as the initial values.
  3. Joint optimisation. The surface point cloud of the object being reconstructed is added to the optimisation as a constraint, giving a collaborative optimisation model of the camera parameters, the projector parameters and the scene’s 3D points.
  4. Corrected extrinsics. With this model the system’s extrinsic parameters are corrected rapidly and accurately.

Results

In the experiments, the technique significantly reduces the reliance on high-precision targets and strict flatness requirements without interrupting the measurement process, and cuts the cost of manual intervention and operation while ensuring reconstruction accuracy and measurement efficiency.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1117/12.3114025.

item.title: Underwater structured-light 3D imaging method based on FP-DiffNet
item.description:
The problem

Fringe-projection profilometry measures shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object and reading the phase of the fringes the camera sees. Its methods and accuracy were established with air as the medium. Under water, several effects act at once. Absorption and scattering attenuate the signal with distance. Small-angle forward scattering from suspended particles blurs the fringes, large-angle backscattering adds background light and noise, and refraction at the water–air interface shifts the light paths. The fringes lose contrast and blur, so phase retrieval accumulates errors and the point cloud can lose regions or be distorted.

Restoration methods such as polarization or stereo imaging rely on prior modelling of the water’s optical parameters, while enhancement methods such as histogram equalization or colour correction can introduce colour bias and extra noise. Deep networks trained end-to-end avoid the priors but act as black boxes without explicit physical constraints, which can distort the restored fringes and bias high-precision phase retrieval.

How it works

FP-DiffNet is a fringe-restoration front end placed between acquisition and phase retrieval. It treats restoration as a conditional denoising diffusion process (DDPM): a U-Net learns to turn noise into a clean fringe image, guided by the degraded underwater image, and a simplified physical model of the degradation keeps the result consistent with underwater light transport. The restored fringes then go through the usual phase-shifting pipeline.

  1. Model the degradation. Following the Jaffe–McGlamery model, the light reaching the camera splits into direct transmission (attenuated with distance), forward scattering (a Gaussian blur of the image) and backscattering (background light and noise). Refraction at the water–air interface adds a depth-dependent shift of the rays.
  2. Train a conditional diffusion model. High-SNR fringe images captured in air are the targets, and fringe images of the same scenes captured in turbid water are the conditions. A clean image is noised towards Gaussian noise over T = 1000 steps, and a U-Net with self-attention learns to predict the injected noise from the noisy image, the step index and the underwater image. The loss combines SSIM, the noise-prediction error, an L1 sparsity term on the weights and a physics-consistency term.
  3. Restore by reverse diffusion. Sampling starts from pure Gaussian noise and removes noise one step at a time, with the underwater observation fed to the network at every step, until a clean fringe image remains.
  4. Correct with physics. A simplified degradation operator, a Gaussian blur for forward scattering plus a noise term for backscattering, links the estimate to the observation. Every k = 50 reverse steps, a gradient step with strength α = 0.01 reduces the residual between the observation and the simulated degradation of the estimate. Refraction is not in this operator; the U-Net learns it from the data.
  5. Retrieve phase and shape. The restored images have the form of standard N-step phase-shifting fringes, so phase retrieval runs unchanged: the arctangent formula gives the wrapped phase, unwrapping gives the absolute phase, and its difference from a reference plane is converted into 3D coordinates with the calibrated projector–camera geometry.

Results

Fringe restoration at the highest turbidity T4: PSNR 42.42 dB, SSIM 0.9750, MS-SSIM 0.9974 (Table 2).
Wrapped-phase MAE 0.0354 rad at T4, 0.0260 rad at T1 (Table 3).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.0890 mm at T4, 0.0317 mm at T1 (Table 4).

The system pairs an industrial camera (1800 × 1600 pixels) with a digital projector (1280 × 1024 pixels) mounted about 0.6 m above an acrylic tank, using a three-frequency four-step phase-shifting scheme. Turbidity was raised by adding 4, 5, 6 and 7 mL of milk to 13 L of clear water, giving four levels T1–T4. The dataset covers five objects in random poses, split 4:1 into 7200 training and 1800 test images, and all reported results are on the test set. Errors are measured against ground-truth fringe images, phases and reconstructions. From T1 to T4, PSNR falls only from 43.02 to 42.42 dB, and wrapped-phase cosine similarity stays between 0.9951 and 0.9962. The remaining phase errors concentrate at object boundaries, shadows and phase discontinuities. Restoring one 512 × 512 fringe image takes about 430 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090.

The authors state the limits. T4 is the most turbid level tested; beyond it they expect restoration to fail once direct transmission falls below the noise floor and the fringe information is lost. The framework applies to sinusoidal phase-shifting patterns, and other structured-light configurations or underwater conditions may need fine-tuning with configuration-specific data.

item.title: Deep transformer-enhanced dynamic structured light for three-dimensional moving object imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a sequence of sinusoidal fringe patterns, each shifted by a known amount, and recovers the 3D shape of a surface from the phase of the captured images. It is robust to ambient light and to changes in surface reflectivity, but it needs at least three images, and the object must stay still while they are taken. If the object moves, each surface point is lit by different projector pixels and seen by different camera pixels in each frame, so the phase steps between frames are no longer the intended ones. The result is ripples, phase-unwrapping errors or a failed reconstruction.

Faster projectors and cameras reduce the problem but raise hardware cost, and the effect of motion still remains. Most error-estimation methods handle motion only along the depth direction and do not address the pixel mismatch caused by motion in other directions. Tracking-based compensation models such as Lu’s work well within the X–Y plane but handle Z-direction motion poorly, and methods that estimate a single global translation miss local, pixel-level motion differences. When an object moves in an arbitrary direction, every surface point has its own displacement and therefore its own phase error.

How it works

The method keeps standard four-step phase shifting and adds two things: a learned tracker that finds where each pixel of one fringe image went in the next ones, and a pixel-wise model of the phase error that remains after that tracking. Both run inside a short sliding window of five frames.

  1. Model the motion-induced phase error. The projector cycles four-step fringes (π/2 apart) while the camera captures the moving object. The motion of each surface point is split into an in-plane displacement, which moves the point to another pixel (Δu, Δv), and a displacement along Z, which adds a phase error. The total phase error is the sum of the two.
  2. Track pixels with a transformer. The image sequence is split into windows of five frames, and the middle frame is the key frame. A COTR (COrrespondence TRansformer) network, initialised with its original pre-trained weights and fine-tuned on fringe images, matches query pixels in the key frame to the other four frames. A shared CNN backbone extracts features from both images, a transformer encoder–decoder relates them, and an MLP head predicts each match.
  3. Align the frames and solve for the Z error. The matches define a pixel-wise mapping that aligns all five frames so the same surface point is followed through the window. Within the short window, the Z-direction velocity is treated as constant, so the Z part of the phase error is (n − 3)ε in frame n. Three intensity combinations of the five frames give three equations in the object phase Φ and ε. For small ε they reduce to a linear equation K1ε + K0 = 0, which is solved at every pixel, and the corrected phase Φ follows.
  4. Unwrap and reconstruct. The corrected wrapped phase is unwrapped with a three-frequency phase-shifting algorithm, using two sets of lower-frequency fringes projected alternately with the high-frequency ones, and converted into 3D shape with the calibrated camera–projector model.
  5. Slide the window. The window moves on by one frame, so each newly acquired image, together with the four before it, gives a new 3D shape of the object.

Results

RMSE 0.072 mm on a moving ceramic plate, against 1.401 mm for standard PSP and 1.352–2.028 mm for Guo’s, Lu’s and Wang’s methods (Section 3.2, Fig. 6).
RMSE 0.096 mm on a moving “Aphrodite” statue, against 1.129 mm for PSP (Section 3.3, Fig. 8).
Fringe-image matching error (AEPE) 0.47–0.83 px for the fine-tuned COTR, against 12.32–21.06 px for optical flow on five unseen objects (Table 1).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.092 mm with COTR as the tracker, against 0.157, 0.181 and 0.490 mm with fine-tuned FlowFormer, GMFlow and RAFT in a combined-motion experiment (Table 2).

The system uses a high-speed camera at 512 × 512 pixels and 30 fps and a DLP projector. To fine-tune COTR, the authors captured 45 dynamic scenes of sculptures, toys and industrial parts on a sandbox, with 60 motions each, giving 2,700 pairs of pre- and post-motion fringe images (2,400 for training, 300 for validation). Ground-truth matches came from an extra blank image projected at each pose, on which a robust local optical flow method computed dense displacements. Training converged after about 1,400 epochs and took about 42 hours.

The ceramic plate was moved by a translation stage at 40° to the camera’s optical axis in 1 mm steps, with a 12-step phase-shifting measurement as ground truth. Standard PSP shows clear ripple distortion. Guo’s method smooths part of it, Lu’s method compensates only motion in the X–Y plane, and Wang’s method simplifies the phase-shift error, which leads to even larger errors. With steps of ±1, ±2 and ±3 mm, the RMS error of the proposed method stays below 0.1 mm (Fig. 6(f)). On the statue, PSP shows stripe artifacts and discontinuities along the edges, Guo’s method still has large errors at the edges, and Lu’s method leaves periodic ripples because Z-direction motion is not compensated; the proposed method recovers the contour more accurately.

The method was also tested on a static statue next to a rotating one, on a rotating fan model with a smooth, weakly textured surface, on a statue on a continuously rotating platform, and on objects that translate and rotate at the same time. Under combined translation and rotation, the rotation adds phase deviations of up to about 1 rad in the outer regions, and the method still keeps most surface areas accurate. The authors note its limits: when the translation along Z is too large, phase-error estimation can still fail (marked regions in Fig. 12); the authors suggest increasing the projection rate or combining the framework with geometry-constraint-based or Gray-code-based unwrapping. Because the estimate relies on a five-frame window, the method works reliably for small inter-frame motion; standard frame rates suffice for slow to moderate motion, while fast objects need high-frame-rate cameras and projectors.

item.title: OPT Projected Structured-Light 3D Cameras
item.description:
The projected structured-light series targets high-precision one-shot reconstruction without a motion platform. It is positioned for dimensional measurement, positioning, bin picking, semiconductor, 3C, lithium battery, and automotive component inspection.

Projected structured-light product matrix covering FPB and FPC series.

My role

My work focuses on the algorithm layer behind this product family: structured-light reconstruction, calibration, point-cloud cleanup, 2D/3D alignment, measurement tools, and Smart3 workflow integration for industrial deployment.

Principle

The camera projects encoded structured light onto the target, captures the deformed stripe or fringe pattern, and reconstructs 3D contour data through decoding, unwrapping, and geometric calibration. The product line is designed for rapid imaging and stable reconstruction under industrial production constraints.

Structured-light projection, encoded patterns, and 3D reconstruction.

Product strengths

The product family emphasizes one-shot imaging, no motion-platform requirement, hardware-side point-cloud output, high-quality projected stripes, multi-projector fusion, multi-exposure fusion, denoising, hole filling, and Smart3 deployment.

Dual projection and telecentric imaging

The high-precision dual-projector route reduces dead zones by projecting from multiple directions. The configuration is reported to reduce imaging blind spots by 95 percent and uses telecentric optics to improve edge stability and Z repeatability in macro measurement tasks.

Dual-projector point-cloud fusion reduces directional blind spots.

2D and 3D alignment

The structured-light products support pixel-level 2D/3D alignment so the same acquisition can serve recognition, defect localization, and 3D measurement. This is useful when classical measurement, AI detection, and point-cloud analysis need to share the same coordinate frame.

Pixel-aligned 2D and 3D output for inspection and measurement.

Applications

Typical applications include toothbrush or workpiece bin picking, headset and sidewall dispensing guidance, semiconductor pin inspection, sealing nail weld inspection, smartphone middle-frame inspection, and high-precision surface bump or dent detection.

One-shot 3D data supports segmentation and robot picking in unordered scenes.

item.title: Calibration Method of Fringe Projection Based on High-Order Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object, recovering the phase of the deformed fringes in the camera image, and converting pixel coordinates and phase into 3D coordinates. That conversion is set by system calibration, and the traditional approaches are laborious. Phase-to-height mapping needs a large, precise calibration target and a precision translation stage, and its parameters depend on how accurately both are made and moved. Stereo-vision calibration takes the target coordinates and their image coordinates in both the camera and the projector, and solves for the parameters by nonlinear optimisation, which is slow, and its accuracy depends on the image coordinates in both the camera and the projector.

A polynomial calibration model avoids the projector model and the translation stage: it directly fits the 3D world coordinates as a polynomial in the pixel coordinates (u, v) and the absolute phase ϕ. Higher orders describe this relationship more accurately, but the number of coefficients grows quickly, and fitting them by least squares becomes slow and unstable once the order exceeds 3. An earlier simplification removes redundant terms by principal component analysis, which speeds the fit up but lowers reconstruction accuracy.

How it works

The method keeps a high-order polynomial calibration model, which needs no projector model and no translation stage, and replaces least-squares fitting with a sparse greedy randomized Kaczmarz (SGRK) solver. SGRK combines the efficient iterations of the randomized sparse Kaczmarz method with the selection strategy of greedy algorithms: each step works on one well-chosen equation instead of the whole system.

  1. Collect calibration points. Fringes are projected onto a circle-grid board placed in several poses. The circle centres are the feature points: each gives its pixel coordinates (u, v), its absolute phase ϕ from three-frequency four-step phase shifting, and its world coordinates from Zhang’s calibration method.
  2. Set up the polynomial model. Each world coordinate X, Y and Z is written as an n-th order polynomial in u, v and ϕ, so calibration becomes a linear system W = Ax. The model has 60 coefficients at order 3, 105 at order 4 and 168 at order 5; the paper uses order 4 as its standard model, balancing accuracy and computing time.
  3. Choose an equation greedily. In each iteration SGRK computes the residual of every equation, keeps the rows whose residual passes a threshold, and draws one of them with probability proportional to its squared residual. Equations with large errors are therefore updated first, which speeds up convergence.
  4. Update and sparsify. The chosen row updates the coefficients by a weighted Kaczmarz projection, and a soft-threshold operation then sets small coefficients to zero, so the solution stays sparse.
  5. Iterate, then reconstruct. The loop runs until the relative error of the coefficients falls below 10⁻⁶. To measure an object, the pixel coordinates and absolute phase of each point are put into the fitted polynomial to give its 3D coordinates.

Results

Standard ceramic sphere (25.0001 mm), 4th-order model: diameter deviation 0.0232 mm in 1.63 s with SGRK, against 0.0727 mm in 3.96 s with least squares (Table 2).
Standard step block, 4th-order model: average errors of 0.004 and −0.003 mm on the two step heights in 1.78 s, against 0.009 and 0.006 mm in 4.32 s with least squares (Table 1).
Ceramic doll: RMSE 0.0729 mm with SGRK versus 0.9250 mm with least squares, measured against a Mech-Eye Pro S Enhanced scan (Sec. 3, Fig. 9).

The system uses a DLP LightCrafter 4500 projector (912 × 1140 pixels), a CCD camera (1280 × 1024 pixels) and a 300 mm × 300 mm circle board with 30 mm between circle centres. Each method was compared on the full 4th-order model and on the PCA-simplified 4th-order model. SGRK was faster and more accurate in both cases: on the sphere the simplified model gave 0.0449 mm in 1.17 s with SGRK against 0.0932 mm in 3.17 s with least squares, and the simplified models were less accurate than the full one for both solvers (Table 2). The step block was measured three times after each calibration to check repeatability (Table 1).

The advantage holds at other orders too (Table 3). At order 3, SGRK gave a sphere diameter deviation of 0.0549 mm in 1.02 s against 0.1470 mm in 3.04 s for least squares; at order 5, 0.0177 mm in 2.31 s against 0.0400 mm in 6.15 s. The 5th-order model is more accurate than the 4th, but its 168 coefficients make the computation markedly longer, and both are more accurate than the 3rd-order model.

item.title: Generative deep-learning-embedded asynchronous structured light for three-dimensional imaging
item.description:
The problem

Structured light measures 3D shape by projecting a sequence of stripe images, called fringe patterns, onto an object and photographing them from a second viewpoint. The surface bends the stripes, and the stripe phase at each pixel encodes depth. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), one of the most popular forms of the technique, the camera must capture each pattern while it alone is on screen. That requires synchronisation between projector and camera, usually a hardware trigger signal.

Synchronisation is a practical burden. Hardware trigger circuits are found in expensive industrial equipment, while affordable consumer devices often have no interface for them, even though the cameras in smartphones, tablets and laptops now offer high resolution and frame rates. Software synchronisation waits longer than the exposure time between patterns, which lowers the frame rate and does not always work stably. Signal wires also limit how far apart camera and projector can be and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. If projector and camera simply run independently, though, the projector can switch patterns in the middle of an exposure, and the photo records a blend of two neighbouring patterns: an aliased fringe pattern (AFP). Computing phase directly from such images leads to reconstruction errors. Earlier work on unsynchronised structured light used simple binary (black-and-white) patterns or addressed other aspects of asynchrony; to the authors’ knowledge, asynchronous capture with the widely used sinusoidal fringes had not been studied.

How it works

The mixing itself has a simple form. Each pixel of an AFP adds up what the two patterns contributed during the exposure, and the split depends on the moment the projector switched (Eq. 5). The mixing does not move pixels; it is the same at every location, a property that suits a convolutional network. The switching moment, however, is unknown and very difficult to measure, so recovering two images from one is an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. The paper treats it as image generation: a generative network learns to produce the two clean patterns, and standard phase-shifting reconstruction then applies unchanged.

  1. Synchronised capture (the reference). Each exposure sees exactly one projected pattern, so each photo holds one clean pattern.
  2. Asynchronous capture. Projector and camera each run at their own constant speed, with the camera faster so that every pattern is captured. A pattern switch inside an exposure produces an AFP that integrates the two neighbouring patterns. The paper addresses mixes of two patterns.
  3. Separation with APSNet. APSNet (aliased fringe pattern separation network) is an encoder–decoder based on U-Net: four encoding blocks with max pooling, then a decoder that upsamples with skip connections back to full resolution. It maps one AFP to the two patterns it was mixed from. It is trained as the generator of a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN): a discriminator judges generated pattern pairs against real ones, and two further loss terms, mean-squared error and structural similarity, keep the generated patterns statistically close to the projected ones. Equal weights for the three terms gave the smoothest training (Fig. 8).
  4. Phase. From three AFPs, APSNet yields four successive patterns, each shifted by a quarter period. The well-established four-step phase-shifting algorithm computes the wrapped phase, and adding the fringe order (multiples of 2π) unwraps it into a continuous phase map.
  5. 3D shape. The continuous phase is converted into the object’s 3D shape with an established FPP reconstruction model.

The training data come from a real system: an industrial camera (2048 × 1536 pixels), a DLP projector (1280 × 1024) and a self-developed microcontroller that delays the camera by a set time Δt after the projector. With Δt = 0 the system captures ordinary, non-aliased fringes. The source patterns were five sets of 256 × 256 sinusoidal fringes with 50 to 90 periods, each in four phase shifts (0, 0.5π, π, 1.5π), captured with delays from 1 to 10 ms in 1 ms steps. This gave 1500 AFPs, each paired with its two source patterns: 1125 for training and 375 for testing.

Results

Within 0.008 mm of the synchronised reconstruction along a depth profile of a statue, with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm. Depth computed directly from the AFPs is off by −5.000 to 3.600 mm, with a standard deviation of 1.713 mm (Fig. 13).
Wrapped phase within 0.035 rad of the synchronised phase along a sampled line (Fig. 11).
Absolute error below 0.006 mm on a propeller and a 3D-printed bolt, objects with large-curvature surfaces absent from the earlier tests (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.001 mm; Fig. 16).

The test objects, including statues, a car model and a sphere, were not seen by the network during training or validation. Every comparison treats the reconstruction from synchronised patterns as the benchmark. Reconstructing directly from the AFPs loses much of the shape, while the shape from APSNet’s patterns is remarkably close to the benchmark (Fig. 12). In the paper’s summary, this improves reconstruction accuracy by three orders of magnitude over using the aliased fringes directly.

The network was trained only on sinusoidal patterns, yet it also separated aliased binary patterns projected onto a sphere, a car model and a statue, without further tuning (Fig. 14). It also handled a multi-object scene of a propeller prototype, a 3D-printed bolt and a statue, with different colours and reflective materials (Fig. 15). The method assumes that each photo mixes two patterns. If the projector runs much faster than the camera, more than two patterns fall within one exposure; the authors name this more complex aliasing as a limitation and a direction for further work.

item.title: Automated reconstruction of multiple objects with individual movement based on PSP
item.description:
The problem

Phase shifting profilometry (PSP) projects several phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns, normally at least three, onto an object and recovers its shape from the phase seen by a camera. Because it needs several images, the object has to stay still while they are captured. If it moves, the captured patterns no longer line up with each other and the designed phase shift between them is violated, so errors appear in the result.

The authors’ earlier work handled movement by describing it with a rotation matrix and a translation vector and building this information into the reconstruction model. It could also reconstruct several isolated objects, but only when they all had the same movement. In practice it is more common for objects to move differently, and existing methods introduce errors when multiple objects with individual movements are reconstructed.

How it works

The method gives every object its own movement description. It first finds the objects, then follows each one through the fringe sequence, computes its rotation and translation separately, and finally retrieves the phase of each object with that object’s movement.

  1. Separate fringes from the object image. The fringe patterns are projected in red and captured by a colour camera. The red component carries the fringes for phase retrieval; in the blue component the fringes are filtered out, leaving a pure object image for tracking and feature extraction.
  2. Identify the objects. In the blue image, the OTSU method separates the objects from the background. Thresholding can split an object into several parts, so a dilation step merges them again, and the contour of each object gives its bounding box.
  3. Track each object with KCF. The object inside each bounding box is used as a template, and the Kernelized Correlation Filters (KCF) tracker finds its new bounding box in the next fringe image. The new box then serves as the template for the images that follow.
  4. Estimate each object’s movement. SIFT finds feature points and their correspondences between the object before and after movement. From these points, singular value decomposition (SVD) gives a rotation matrix and translation vector for each object.
  5. Reconstruct object by object. With its own movement information, the phase of each object is retrieved from the red component by a least-squares solution of the reconstruction model that includes the movement, and the object is reconstructed. This repeats until the last object is done.

Results

RMS error 0.0773 mm with the proposed method, against 8.981 mm with traditional PSP, for two car models moving individually (Section 4, Fig. 10).

The experiment uses a colour camera (Allied Vision Manta 504C, 2452 × 2056) and a projector (Wintech DLP PRO 4500, 912 × 1140). Two car models are measured with 3-step PSP using red fringes while each one rotates and translates on the reference plane in its own way. The reference is a 6-step PSP reconstruction of the static objects. Traditional PSP shows clear movement-induced errors, which are most serious where the height changes sharply, such as at the edges of the objects; with the proposed method these errors are removed. The method can also reconstruct only selected objects and ignore the others, by choosing the objects of interest after identification.

The authors state the conditions of the method. It considers only rigid objects with two-dimensional movement. Object identification works best with a large enough intensity difference between objects and background, and because dilation enlarges the objects, they must keep some distance from each other. The fringe colour should differ strongly from the object colour, and when ambient light is weak, blue background light should be added to the projected pattern. There is no limit on movement speed, but the capture must be fast enough to give clear images.

item.title: 3D Autoscan System
item.description:
A scanner + rotary platform pipeline that captures arbitrary objects to ~0.1 mm in under five minutes — built to seed a 3D shape database without per-object parameter tuning.

Figure 1. Scanner + rotary platform setup. Controlled by a single PC running the registration pipeline.

Problem

Building a 3D shape database requires scanning many objects. Off-the-shelf scanning is fine for one model, but at database scale it costs human hours: every object shape requires re-tuning algorithm parameters, and every mis-registration eats into the ~5 min/object budget. The need is a robust pipeline that adapts — per-object parameter tuning has to disappear.

Pipeline

The system fuses three algorithmic stages tuned to handle scale, reflectance, and pose variation without manual intervention.

Frame-to-frame registration aligns sequential scans on both geometry and texture; an outlier removal stage strips away background noise; finally a global registration pass aligns the multiple platform poses into a coherent model.
